1. Rich newcomers moving into an old neighbourhood is a textbook case of GENTRIFICATION, frequently displacing long-standing low-income residents. — GENTRIFICATION (danh từ) = sự cải tạo đô thị làm tăng giá và đẩy người thu nhập thấp ra ngoài; collocation thường gặp: "drive/resist gentrification", "neighbourhood gentrification".

2. During rush hour, the roads downtown descend into full GRIDLOCK, with no vehicle able to move in any direction. — GRIDLOCK (danh từ không đếm được) = tắc nghẽn giao thông hoàn toàn; không thêm "s"; collocation: "traffic gridlock", "cause gridlock".

3. Years of neglect have left many of the buildings along the riverfront DILAPIDATED. — DILAPIDATED (tính từ) = xuống cấp, đổ nát do bị bỏ bê; chỉ dùng cho công trình/vật thể, không dùng cho người; collocation: "dilapidated housing/slums".

4. Surveillance cameras have become UBIQUITOUS across almost every street corner of the city. — UBIQUITOUS (tính từ tuyệt đối) = có mặt khắp nơi; tránh dùng với "very/more"; collocation: "become ubiquitous", "a ubiquitous feature".

5. Many residents of sprawling housing blocks report a quiet sense of ALIENATION from their neighbours. — ALIENATION (danh từ) = cảm giác cô lập, lạc lõng; đi với giới từ "from" khi chỉ rõ đối tượng, không dùng "of"; collocation: "a sense of alienation".

6. The MUNICIPAL authorities have been criticised for failing to expand public services fast enough to match population growth. — MUNICIPAL (tính từ) = thuộc về thành phố/chính quyền địa phương; không dùng như danh từ; collocation: "municipal authorities/infrastructure".

7. Rapid URBANISATION is drawing more people from the countryside into towns and cities each year, raising pressure on housing and transport. — URBANISATION (danh từ, chính tả Anh dùng -s-) = quá trình đô thị hoá; collocation: "rapid urbanisation", "drive urbanisation".

8. Unchecked urban SPRAWL has swallowed up thousands of hectares of green land on the city's periphery. — SPRAWL (danh từ, hàm ý tiêu cực) = sự lan rộng đô thị thiếu quy hoạch; collocation: "urban sprawl", "unchecked sprawl".

9. City planners argue that more parks and public amenities would significantly enhance the capital's LIVEABILITY. — LIVEABILITY (danh từ, chính tả Anh giữ "e") = mức độ đáng sống của một nơi; collocation: "enhance/restore a city's liveability".

10. Severe OVERCROWDING, with too many people crammed into too few flats, has put serious strain on the district's water and electricity supply. — OVERCROWDING (danh từ không đếm được) = tình trạng quá tải dân số; tính từ tương ứng là "overcrowded"; collocation: "tackle overcrowding".

11. With barely a tree or a park in sight, the downtown area can feel like a depressing CONCRETE JUNGLE. — CONCRETE JUNGLE (idiom, cụm cố định) = "rừng bê tông", chỉ đô thị chật chội thiếu cây xanh; ít khi chia số nhiều trừ khi so sánh nhiều thành phố; collocation: "escape the concrete jungle".

12. A severe HOUSING CRISIS has left thousands of young families unable to find suitable, affordable accommodation. — HOUSING CRISIS (danh từ ghép, không chèn "of" ở giữa) = khủng hoảng nhà ở do thiếu nhà giá phải chăng; collocation: "tackle/exacerbate the housing crisis".

passages.text: When the Sorbonne urbanist Carlos Moreno first set out his proposal for the "fifteen-minute city" in 2016, it was a quiet, almost technical paper about chrono-urbanism: a city should be reorganised so that residents could reach work, schools, clinics, shops and green space within a quarter-hour walk or cycle from home. By the close of the decade, the same idea had become the centrepiece of municipal manifestos from Paris to Bogota, and a magnet for accusations ranging from urban elitism to outright surveillance. The arc, according to Moreno himself, has revealed less about the merits of proximity planning than about the political climate into which any contemporary urban proposal must now be inserted.

At its most defensible, the concept is a synthesis of two older traditions: the neighbourhood-unit theory of the 1920s and the compact-city literature that flourished after the 1990 Brundtland framework. Its appeal in the early 2020s, however, rested on a more pressing concern. Cities across the temperate zone had begun to register summer surface temperatures five to seven degrees Celsius above their rural surroundings, a phenomenon known as the urban heat island. According to climatologist Brian Stone of Georgia Tech, the combination of asphalt, low albedo and waste heat from engines now contributes more to local warming in many North American cities than the background signal of global climate change. Reducing motorised trips, narrowing carriageways and replacing impervious surfaces with vegetation became, in this framing, less a matter of taste than a measure of public-health policy.

Quantifying the gain, however, has proved unexpectedly difficult. A 2022 modelling study by the urban-climatology group at ETH Zurich estimated that converting one third of central Zurich's streets into shaded mixed-use corridors could reduce peak heat exposure by 1.4 degrees Celsius for the median pedestrian. Yet the same study cautioned that the gain depended on canopy cover reaching maturity, a process which in temperate climates may take fifteen to twenty years. The figure also masked considerable variation between districts: south-facing streets with narrow widths recorded gains nearly double those of broader east-west axes, suggesting that any aggregate estimate conceals a patchwork of micro-climates. Critics, including the transport economist Jose Gomez-Ibanez at Harvard, have argued that proximity-based interventions tend to underestimate the time lag between a redesign and its measurable effect on health outcomes, and that voters rarely have the patience to wait for arboreal time. The argument is not that the model is wrong but that the political horizon of urban administrations is structurally too short to bear the wait.

A second line of objection concerns who benefits. The geographer Jennifer Robinson at University College London has noted that fifteen-minute neighbourhoods, when superimposed on already segregated metropolitan regions, may entrench rather than dissolve inequality. If the only districts in which the model is feasible are those with existing density, mixed zoning and decent transit, the policy risks becoming an amenity for the already advantaged. Robinson's own fieldwork in Johannesburg and Mumbai suggests that fragmented peripheries cannot simply be re-stitched by aesthetic interventions; the underlying problem is the unequal distribution of services that long predates any planning fashion. Proponents counter that nothing in Moreno's original framework prohibits its application to lower-income districts, and indeed Paris invested most heavily in its outer arrondissements between 2020 and 2023. The empirical question of where benefits actually accrue remains, in much of the literature, unresolved.

The most arresting recent twist has been ideological. From late 2022, a loose network of online commentators began to describe fifteen-minute neighbourhoods as a vehicle for movement restriction, often by conflating Moreno's proposal with traffic-filter trials in Oxford and Canterbury. The two policies are, in fact, distinct: a low-traffic neighbourhood limits through-traffic on certain streets, whereas the fifteen-minute city merely seeks to bring services within walking range. Yet the conflation has been politically consequential. Polling by the Centre for Cities in 2023 indicated that public support for any scheme labelled "fifteen-minute" had fallen by eleven percentage points in the United Kingdom over twelve months, even where the underlying measures remained popular when described in neutral terms. The episode is a reminder, in the view of urbanist Samuel Stein, that contemporary planning vocabulary is now contested terrain in itself.

Some climate-adaptation researchers argue, in any case, that proximity planning is a necessary but insufficient response. Even a fully realised fifteen-minute district will not, on its own, neutralise a 45-degree heatwave. The wider package, according to a 2024 review by the C40 Cities network, must include cool-roof mandates, the daylighting of buried streams, and significant tree-canopy targets enforced at the parcel scale. Where such measures have been combined with proximity planning, as in Medellin's Green Corridors programme, ambient temperatures have fallen by an average of two degrees Celsius and respiratory admissions in adjacent clinics have declined. Where proximity has been pursued without the accompanying ecological infrastructure, the heat gains have tended to be marginal.

What is striking, then, is not that the fifteen-minute city is either solution or trojan horse, but that it is being asked to carry an unusually heavy argumentative load. It is, simultaneously, a climate-adaptation strategy, a public-health intervention, a democratic claim about who the street belongs to, and a target of cultural anxiety. None of these readings is wholly wrong, and none, on the available evidence, is fully sufficient. Whether the model survives the present decade may depend less on the elegance of its diagrams than on the willingness of municipalities to defend a planning vocabulary which they have, until recently, treated as technical rather than political. Defending that vocabulary, Moreno has suggested in subsequent writing, will mean accepting that even modest interventions in the urban fabric are now read as ideological statements, and that the technocratic neutrality once claimed by planners may no longer be available.

audio_scripts.text: Good afternoon, everyone. Today's lecture continues our urban climatology series, and I want to focus on the empirical literature concerning the urban heat island phenomenon and its smart-city mitigation. [pause:5s] The framework I'll be drawing on comes from the work of Professor Adaeze Okereke — that's O-K-E-R-E-K-E, no hyphen, single word. Okereke's 2019 monograph reframed urban heat from a single-metric anomaly into what she terms the "thermal load mosaic". [pause:3s] Firstly, a brief historical orientation. The longitudinal sensor network I'll reference today was first deployed in 2014 — sorry, let me correct that, 2013; the published descriptive analysis in 2014 covered data collected over the preceding year, so 2013. Whenever I refer to the baseline year, please record 2013. [pause:3s] Right. A quick tense-orientation note before we get into the substance. Okereke's mosaic concept USED TO be operationalised with fixed rooftop stations only, NOW the field deploys distributed low-cost sensor swarms feeding real-time municipal dashboards, and from 2028 a pan-European consortium WILL be embedding satellite-thermal layers in the same data pipeline. So past, present, future. For today's purposes I'm focusing on the CURRENT methodological state — that is, distributed sensor swarms. [pause:3s] Moving to terminology. The micro-zone concept Okereke foregrounds — a sub-neighbourhood patch whose surface temperature decouples from the broader urban field — is termed a "thermal cell". Now, you'll encounter related labels in the older literature: heat pocket, warm spot, micro-anomaly. All of these gesture toward overlapping phenomena, but they are NOT interchangeable with Okereke's term. The currently accepted scholarly term is thermal cell — t-h-e-r-m-a-l cell. So when the older literature uses heat pocket or warm spot, that's a related but distinct construct. [pause:3s] The next domain I want to discuss is what urban climatologists call the "mitigation typology". When practitioners describe how cities respond to summer-peak temperatures, they sketch a graded typology running from reflective albedo treatments through evapotranspirative greening to active mechanical cooling. So, you know, you'll see boroughs that simply paint roofs white — that's albedo treatment. Or districts that pilot rooftop wetland strips — that's evapotranspirative greening. Now, these are illustrative cases, not the technical term itself. The umbrella term is the mitigation typology. [pause:3s] Now, the sensor data — and this is where I want you to pay close attention, because the quantifiers cluster densely here. Of the four hundred thermal cells we instrumented across six European cities last summer, MOST recorded peak surface temperatures above the safety threshold — roughly sixty-eight per cent. Only a few — about eleven per cent — stayed within the comfort envelope, and some — twenty-one per cent — fluctuated near the threshold. So overheating dominates numerically, but the threshold-fluctuating tail, though modest, is operationally significant for early-warning protocols. [pause:3s] A second key construct I want to flag is "diurnal lag". This refers to a temporal pattern in which dense built fabric releases stored daytime heat several hours into the night — sometimes prolonging hazardous conditions until two in the morning. At Riverside ward, our sensor array logged eighty-two documented diurnal-lag episodes across the cohort during one summer. [pause:3s] Crucially, the assumption that vegetation density linearly reduces ambient warming is, frankly, not supported. Most of the thermal cells in our sample did NOT show the predicted monotonic cooling as canopy cover increased. Quite the opposite — many showed a U-shaped curve, with a re-warming spike around the seventy-per-cent canopy mark, because dense canopies trap nocturnal heat. So the older "linear greening" hypothesis, which predicts continuous cooling, is empirically NOT corroborated by our data. [pause:3s] Let me return to something I touched on earlier — the methodological tense-orientation point I made at the start. That CURRENT distributed-swarm state is what we're, kinda, gonna scrutinise in this afternoon's practical. I want you to focus on the sensor-calibration protocols specifically, not the satellite-thermal futures or the legacy rooftop instruments. [pause:3s] To summarise: urban heat is a mosaic, not a single metric; the technical term for a sub-neighbourhood decoupled patch is thermal cell; overheating dominates the cohort at roughly sixty-eight per cent; and the linear greening hypothesis is not empirically supported. Next week we'll examine social-vulnerability indices. Thank you. [pause:3s] (Q1) (Q2) (Q3) (Q4) (Q5) (Q6)

blocks.text: The line graph compares the urban population, in millions, of four megacities — Tokyo, Delhi, Lagos and Sao Paulo — over a fifty-year period from 1975 to 2025.

Overall, while Tokyo retained its status as the largest urban agglomeration throughout, its growth plateaued, whereas Delhi and Lagos underwent the most dramatic megacity expansion. Sao Paulo, by contrast, followed a comparatively moderate urbanisation trajectory across the period.

In 1975, Tokyo already housed approximately 26.6 million inhabitants, dwarfing the other three cities, which ranged between 1.9 and 10.7 million. Tokyo subsequently rose steadily to a peak of 38.1 million in 2015 before edging downward to 37.2 million, suggesting that demographic concentration may have levelled off. Sao Paulo, meanwhile, expanded gently from 10.7 to 22.4 million.

Delhi, however, surged almost eight-fold, climbing from 4.4 million to roughly 33.8 million and nearly converging with Tokyo by 2025. Lagos exhibited the steepest relative curve, rising off a low base of 1.9 million to around 21.0 million and drawing almost level with Sao Paulo by 2025 without ever overtaking it, largely owing to relentless peri-urban growth.
The line graph charts the urban population, in millions, of four megacities — Tokyo, Delhi, Lagos and Sao Paulo — between 1975 and 2025.

Overall, a clear contrast emerges between the mature agglomeration and the emerging ones: Tokyo, though consistently the most populous, all but plateaued, whereas Delhi and Lagos expanded explosively and Sao Paulo advanced at a more sedate pace. The half-century thus narrowed a once-vast gulf between the established and the rising megacities.

Tokyo opened far ahead, at 26.6 million, and crept up to a peak of 38.1 million in 2015 before slipping to 37.2 million — a trajectory typical of a saturated, ageing economy. Sao Paulo traced a gentler arc, rising steadily from 10.7 to 22.4 million.

The Asian and African cities, by contrast, transformed the picture entirely. Delhi rocketed almost eight-fold, from 4.4 to 33.8 million, all but converging on Tokyo by 2025; Lagos, climbing off a negligible 1.9 million to some 21.0 million, registered the steepest relative ascent of all, drawing almost level with Sao Paulo by 2025 yet never overtaking it. So precipitous was this growth that the gap separating the largest and smallest cities had contracted dramatically.

blocks.text: Cities function as engines of opportunity, offering agglomeration benefits such as concentrated job markets, world-class healthcare and a dazzling array of cultural amenities within a single metropolis.

Dense urban living can, somewhat counter-intuitively, be more environmentally efficient than dispersed suburban sprawl, since shared public transport and compact housing lower the per-capita carbon footprint.

The proximity of diverse industries and universities in a metropolis fosters innovation, as professionals and entrepreneurs cross-pollinate ideas far more readily than they could in isolated rural communities.

Investment in public infrastructure and essential amenities, from libraries to healthcare clinics, tends to be more cost-effective when concentrated in a single urban centre rather than spread thinly across the countryside.
Chronic traffic congestion has become an intractable feature of sprawling metropolitan areas, eating into residents' leisure time and swelling their daily commute.
Severe overcrowding in fast-growing cities places immense strain on housing stock, often forcing newcomers into cramped, substandard accommodation.
The relentless pace of urban life, compounded by a pervasive sense of alienation, can take a considerable psychological toll on residents who feel anonymous amid the crowds.
Exorbitant property prices in sought-after neighbourhoods have priced an entire generation of young professionals out of homeownership.
Sustained rural-to-urban migration, driven by the search for better wages and superior educational institutions, continues to swell the population of major cities well beyond their planned capacity.
Rapid urbanisation in developing economies is fuelled by the perception that a cosmopolitan lifestyle offers advantages unavailable in the countryside, from career prospects to modern healthcare.
A chronic lack of affordable housing stems partly from restrictive zoning laws that limit the construction of higher-density residential buildings near city centres.
Weak long-term planning means that municipal authorities frequently fail to expand transport and utility networks in step with population growth, leaving infrastructure perpetually playing catch-up.
Unchecked arrivals into saturated urban cores fuel the proliferation of dilapidated housing on the periphery, where sanitation and safety standards are frequently substandard.
The skyrocketing cost of living in major cities has pushed many working-class families towards the outskirts, lengthening their commutes and eroding their quality of life.
Gentrification frequently displaces long-standing low-income communities, as rising rents and property taxes make once-affordable neighbourhoods unrecognisable within a matter of years.
Prolonged exposure to gridlock and overcrowding has been linked to heightened stress levels, undermining both the mental health and productivity of the urban workforce.
Municipal governments must grapple with the seemingly irreconcilable demands of accommodating population growth while preserving green spaces and historic neighbourhoods.
Bridging the widening gap between affluent enclaves and marginalised peripheries remains one of the most persistent challenges facing city planners today.
Tackling the housing crisis without triggering further speculation in the property market requires a delicate balancing act that few administrations have mastered.
Reconciling the need for higher-density development with residents' resistance to construction near their homes continues to stall much-needed infrastructure projects.

idea_sections.heading: 5. Problems / Challenges — Vấn đề / Thách thức

blocks.text: The strategic decentralisation of economic activity, achieved by building satellite towns with their own industries and universities, could plausibly redirect migration away from saturated capitals.
Heavily subsidising mass transit, in tandem with congestion charging on private vehicles entering the city centre, would make public transport more attractive than driving.
The 15-minute city model, in which essential services are reachable on foot or by bike, could markedly reduce reliance on motorised commuting and enhance neighbourhood liveability.
Expanding affordable housing schemes and easing restrictive zoning regulations would help absorb population growth without triggering runaway property prices.
Many urban planners increasingly advocate compact, walkable neighbourhoods over car-dependent urban sprawl, arguing that density need not come at the expense of quality of life.
A significant proportion of city dwellers regard the daily struggle with gridlock and overcrowded public transport as an unavoidable price of urban convenience.
There is a common perception that escaping the concrete jungle for a quieter, more affordable rural existence is becoming increasingly appealing to younger generations.
Some commentators contend that gentrification is, on balance, a positive force, since it revitalises decaying neighbourhoods and reduces local crime, even as it displaces long-term residents.

idea_sections.heading: 7. Popular opinions — Quan điểm phổ biến

blocks.text: Municipal authorities bear primary responsibility for scaling infrastructure investment in line with population growth rather than reacting only once congestion becomes unmanageable.
National governments have a duty to fund large-scale infrastructure projects, such as mass transit networks, that individual cities often cannot finance alone.
Property developers and local councils share responsibility for ensuring that new developments include a meaningful proportion of affordable housing rather than exclusively high-end units.
Ordinary residents, too, hold some responsibility for supporting higher-density housing near their own neighbourhoods rather than resisting development that could ease the wider housing crisis.

idea_sections.heading: 8. Who is responsible — Trách nhiệm thuộc về ai

blocks.text: Although gentrification is routinely criticised for displacing long-standing residents, some argue that the resulting economic revitalisation brings investment and jobs that ultimately benefit the wider community.

While decentralisation is often proposed as a cure for overcrowding, critics point out that satellite towns lacking genuine employment ecosystems risk becoming mere dormitory suburbs rather than self-sufficient hubs.
It could be argued that congestion charging unfairly penalises lower-income commuters who cannot afford to live near their workplaces, even as it succeeds in easing traffic congestion.
Sceptics of the 15-minute city concept warn that concentrating amenities within small zones could inadvertently fragment cities into isolated pockets, undermining the sense of a unified metropolis.
As remote and hybrid working arrangements become ubiquitous, growing numbers of professionals may relocate away from exorbitant city-centre rents towards more affordable suburban or rural areas.
Smart-city technologies that monitor traffic flow and energy use in real time are likely to become a standard feature of municipal infrastructure within the coming decades.
There is growing evidence that climate resilience will increasingly shape urban planning, with cities investing in green corridors and flood defences alongside conventional infrastructure.

The continued urbanisation trajectory across much of the developing world suggests that megacities will keep expanding, intensifying pressure on housing, transport and public services for the foreseeable future.

idea_sections.heading: 10. Future trends / predictions — Xu hướng tương lai

blocks.text: Whereas previous generations tolerated long, gruelling commutes as an inevitable feature of city life, today's workforce increasingly prioritises liveability and proximity over sheer career opportunity.
Compact, transit-oriented cities generally cope with population growth far more gracefully than car-dependent metropolises characterised by unchecked urban sprawl.
Cities that have invested heavily in mass transit and cycling infrastructure tend to report markedly lower congestion than comparable cities that have prioritised road-building for private vehicles.
Unlike the affluent districts of a city, which enjoy abundant green space and reliable services, peripheral neighbourhoods often make do with patchy amenities and ageing infrastructure.
A personal anecdote about a family that relocated from a dilapidated inner-city neighbourhood to a satellite town in search of more affordable housing and cleaner air.
Case studies of cities that have introduced congestion charging, illustrating how such schemes can simultaneously curb private car use and generate revenue for transit expansion.
Longitudinal urban-planning research tracking how gentrification reshapes the demographic composition and property values of a neighbourhood over successive decades.

Comparative observations of cities that have adopted the 15-minute city framework versus those still organised around car-centric, low-density development, highlighting differences in residents' daily quality of life.

idea_sections.heading: 12. Examples / evidence types — Loại ví dụ / minh chứng

blocks.text: Urban overcrowding has emerged as a defining issue of the twenty-first century, particularly across rapidly developing economies. In my view, this phenomenon stems chiefly from unchecked rural-to-urban migration and inadequate municipal planning, although a combination of targeted policies could reasonably alleviate the pressure.

It is rural migration, more than any other factor, that has paved the way for today's overcrowded metropolises. Young workers tend to flock to capital cities in search of better employment opportunities and superior educational amenities, leaving the countryside hollowed out. A second cause, arguably just as significant, is the failure of municipal authorities to expand transport infrastructure at the same pace as population growth. In many fast-growing cities, the subway network has barely changed in fifteen years even though the population has nearly doubled, a clear case of planning lagging behind demographic reality.

Turning to solutions, governments should, in my opinion, decentralise economic activity by developing satellite towns with their own industries and universities. This would, to some extent, redirect migrants away from saturated centres. Equally important is heavy subsidisation of mass transit; only when buses and trains become more reliable than private cars will commuters genuinely abandon their vehicles. The 15-minute city model, which Paris has experimented with, also seems a promising blueprint, as it ensures residents can reach work, schools and healthcare within walking distance.

In conclusion, the overcrowding crisis is largely driven by migration patterns and weak infrastructure planning, and it is through decentralisation and investment in public transit that meaningful improvement can occur. While no single measure can solve the problem overnight, a coordinated approach could plausibly relieve the strain that megacities currently face.

Few urban phenomena are as pressing as the relentless overcrowding of contemporary cities, a trend driven by intersecting economic and demographic forces. While the underlying causes are well documented, the solutions demand far greater political will than is typically acknowledged.

The principal driver, it would appear, is the powerful economic pull of metropolises, where wages, healthcare amenities and cosmopolitan lifestyles vastly outstrip those of rural regions. Compounding this is the chronic inability of municipal authorities to scale infrastructure in step with arrivals; the result is gridlock, the proliferation of dilapidated slums, and rising psychological alienation among long-term residents. Not only does inadequate planning intensify daily commutes, but it also widens the chasm between affluent enclaves and marginalised peripheries, a divide that fuels long-term social instability.

A multifaceted response is required. The strategic decentralisation of economic activity, through the construction of satellite hubs with their own employment ecosystems, could plausibly redirect migration flows. Complementing this, the introduction of congestion charging, with Stockholm and London as instructive precedents, has been shown to curb private car usage while generating revenue for transit expansion. Equally compelling is the 15-minute city framework, under which essential services are reachable on foot, thereby reducing reliance on motorised commuting and, in the process, lowering the carbon footprint of the urban core. So overwhelming is the case for investment in mass transit that any government failing to subsidise it heavily risks condemning its cities to permanent gridlock, while squandering the agglomeration benefits that drew migrants in the first place.

In conclusion, the overcrowding crisis is, in essence, a planning failure rather than an inevitable consequence of growth. Through the deliberate distribution of opportunity, the disincentivisation of private vehicles and the redesign of neighbourhoods around walkability, policymakers can, in all likelihood, restore liveability to the urban environment, provided, of course, that short-term electoral pressures do not derail long-term strategy.

Phần A — Viết lại câu

1. Rich newcomers moving into an old neighbourhood is a textbook case of GENTRIFICATION, frequently displacing long-standing low-income residents. — GENTRIFICATION (danh từ) = sự cải tạo đô thị làm tăng giá và đẩy người thu nhập thấp ra ngoài; collocation thường gặp: "drive/resist gentrification", "neighbourhood gentrification".

2. During rush hour, the roads downtown descend into full GRIDLOCK, with no vehicle able to move in any direction. — GRIDLOCK (danh từ không đếm được) = tắc nghẽn giao thông hoàn toàn; không thêm "s"; collocation: "traffic gridlock", "cause gridlock".

3. Years of neglect have left many of the buildings along the riverfront DILAPIDATED. — DILAPIDATED (tính từ) = xuống cấp, đổ nát do bị bỏ bê; chỉ dùng cho công trình/vật thể, không dùng cho người; collocation: "dilapidated housing/slums".

4. Surveillance cameras have become UBIQUITOUS across almost every street corner of the city. — UBIQUITOUS (tính từ tuyệt đối) = có mặt khắp nơi; tránh dùng với "very/more"; collocation: "become ubiquitous", "a ubiquitous feature".

5. Many residents of sprawling housing blocks report a quiet sense of ALIENATION from their neighbours. — ALIENATION (danh từ) = cảm giác cô lập, lạc lõng; đi với giới từ "from" khi chỉ rõ đối tượng, không dùng "of"; collocation: "a sense of alienation".

6. The MUNICIPAL authorities have been criticised for failing to expand public services fast enough to match population growth. — MUNICIPAL (tính từ) = thuộc về thành phố/chính quyền địa phương; không dùng như danh từ; collocation: "municipal authorities/infrastructure".

7. Rapid URBANISATION is drawing more people from the countryside into towns and cities each year, raising pressure on housing and transport. — URBANISATION (danh từ, chính tả Anh dùng -s-) = quá trình đô thị hoá; collocation: "rapid urbanisation", "drive urbanisation".

8. Unchecked urban SPRAWL has swallowed up thousands of hectares of green land on the city's periphery. — SPRAWL (danh từ, hàm ý tiêu cực) = sự lan rộng đô thị thiếu quy hoạch; collocation: "urban sprawl", "unchecked sprawl".

9. City planners argue that more parks and public amenities would significantly enhance the capital's LIVEABILITY. — LIVEABILITY (danh từ, chính tả Anh giữ "e") = mức độ đáng sống của một nơi; collocation: "enhance/restore a city's liveability".

10. Severe OVERCROWDING, with too many people crammed into too few flats, has put serious strain on the district's water and electricity supply. — OVERCROWDING (danh từ không đếm được) = tình trạng quá tải dân số; tính từ tương ứng là "overcrowded"; collocation: "tackle overcrowding".

11. With barely a tree or a park in sight, the downtown area can feel like a depressing CONCRETE JUNGLE. — CONCRETE JUNGLE (idiom, cụm cố định) = "rừng bê tông", chỉ đô thị chật chội thiếu cây xanh; ít khi chia số nhiều trừ khi so sánh nhiều thành phố; collocation: "escape the concrete jungle".

12. A severe HOUSING CRISIS has left thousands of young families unable to find suitable, affordable accommodation. — HOUSING CRISIS (danh từ ghép, không chèn "of" ở giữa) = khủng hoảng nhà ở do thiếu nhà giá phải chăng; collocation: "tackle/exacerbate the housing crisis".
Phần B — Nâng cấp câu
1. Band 7: Rapid urbanisation is causing severe overcrowding in cities across the world.
Band 8: Rapid urbanisation has rendered chronic overcrowding an almost inescapable feature of the modern metropolis, straining housing, transport and public infrastructure alike.
2. Band 7: There is a persistent lack of affordable housing for ordinary working people.
Band 8: So acute is the shortage of affordable housing that even full-time workers on median incomes are routinely priced out of the cities in which they are employed.
3. Band 7: Old neighbourhoods often undergo rapid gentrification once wealthier residents begin moving in.

Band 8: Once affluent newcomers move in, gentrification frequently sets in motion a chain reaction of rising rents and property taxes, gradually displacing the very communities that gave the neighbourhood its character.
4. Band 7: Governments need to invest more heavily in transport infrastructure to keep pace with urban growth.
Band 8: Not until municipal authorities invest substantially in infrastructure will chronic congestion cease to be an intractable feature of the sprawling metropolis.
5. Band 7: Living far from the city centre can leave residents feeling isolated from the wider community.
Band 8: The further residents are pushed to the periphery, the more pronounced their sense of alienation from the wider urban community tends to become.
6. Band 7: Some cities are expanding outwards into the countryside rather than building upwards.
Band 8: Rather than densifying existing districts, many cities have succumbed to unchecked urban sprawl, encroaching relentlessly upon the surrounding countryside.
7. Band 7: Relocating jobs and services away from the city centre could help relieve pressure on the capital.
Band 8: Were economic activity to be strategically decentralised into satellite hubs, migration pressure on the capital could plausibly be redirected rather than merely contained.
8. Band 7: A city with abundant parks, clean air and reliable public services offers a far higher standard of liveability.
Band 8: It is precisely the interplay of green space, clean air and robust public amenities that elevates a city's liveability from merely tolerable to genuinely desirable.

blocks.text: 1. Facts & Trends (Dữ liệu thực tế để support cho bài Writing)
The Rise of Megacities: A megacity has a population of over 10 million. By 2030, it is projected that there will be over 40 megacities globally, primarily in Asia and Africa.

The "15-Minute City" Concept: An urban planning model where essential amenities (work, schools, healthcare, shops) are all accessible within a 15-minute walk or bike ride, aiming to reduce car reliance and carbon emissions.
Telecommuting and Decentralization: The post-pandemic shift towards remote work is encouraging some people to leave the exorbitant cost of the metropolis for more affordable suburban or rural areas.
2. Main Ideas Bank (Arguments)
Topic: Urbanization (Rural to Urban Migration)

Causes: The search for better employment opportunities (economic pull factors); access to superior educational institutions and healthcare amenities; the allure of a cosmopolitan lifestyle (bright lights, big city).
Effects: Severe strain on municipal infrastructure; the proliferation of dilapidated slums due to a lack of affordable housing; a brain drain in rural areas, leaving agriculture sector struggling.
Topic: Tackling Traffic Congestion
Solution 1 (Public Transport): Governments must heavily subsidise mass transit systems (subways, trams) to make them cheaper and more reliable than private car ownership.
Solution 2 (Congestion Charging): Imposing hefty fees on vehicles entering the city centre during peak hours acts as a powerful deterrent, simultaneously raising funds for road maintenance.
Solution 3 (Urban Design): Pedestrianising city centres and building dedicated cycling lanes to encourage eco-friendly commuting.
Topic: Gentrification (Is it positive or negative?)
Positives (Revitalization): Cleans up dilapidated neighbourhoods; reduces local crime rates; boosts the local economy by attracting new businesses, cafes, and investments.

Negatives (Displacement): Exacerbates the housing crisis by driving up property taxes and rent; destroys the original cultural identity of the area; forces long-term, low-income residents into worse living conditions elsewhere.
(Mệnh đề quan hệ đi kèm giới từ - "Vũ khí" ngữ pháp siêu học thuật để miêu tả không gian, lý do, hoặc phương tiện trong IELTS Writing Task 2)

What I'd like to talk about is Tay Ho, a lakeside district in northwest Hanoi that, in my view, embodies pretty much everything a thoughtfully designed neighbourhood should offer. Bordered by the eleven-square-kilometre West Lake, it's a pocket of the metropolis where the manic gridlock of downtown gives way to tree-lined avenues and a far more breathable urban fabric.

Aesthetically, the area is a fascinating juxtaposition of vernacular architecture — narrow tube houses and centuries-old pagodas — alongside contemporary low-rise apartments built around shared courtyards. What strikes me most is how walkable it feels; essential amenities like markets, cafes, and clinics are all within a fifteen-minute stroll, which mirrors the so-called "15-minute city" model pioneered by Paris under Anne Hidalgo back in 2020.

As for the residents, it's a remarkably cosmopolitan mix: long-standing Vietnamese families coexist with expatriates, artists, and remote workers, lending the area a creative, slightly bohemian atmosphere without the alienation you'd normally associate with sprawling megacities.

The reason I find it so appealing boils down to three factors. Firstly, the proximity to nature significantly mitigates the psychological toll of urban living — research from the University of Exeter suggests just two hours weekly in green spaces measurably improves wellbeing. Secondly, the neighbourhood has somehow managed to revitalize itself without succumbing to aggressive gentrification, retaining its cultural identity. And thirdly, what really sells it for me is the sense of community; rarely have I encountered an urban district where neighbours actually know each other by name.
All in all, were I given the means to relocate tomorrow, Tay Ho would unquestionably be my first choice — it strikes that elusive balance between connectivity and liveability.

blocks.text: Q1: Should governments limit urban migration?

Point: I'd argue that imposing outright restrictions on urban migration is both ethically questionable and practically counterproductive, though some form of demand management is undoubtedly warranted.

Explain: The fundamental issue is that rural-to-urban migration is largely a symptom of regional inequality rather than a cause of urban dysfunction. Heavy-handed restrictions — such as China's hukou household registration system — tend to create a two-tiered citizenship where migrants are denied access to public services, which actually exacerbates urban poverty rather than alleviating it.

Example: Take Shenzhen, for instance: despite decades of population caps, the city ballooned from 30,000 residents in 1980 to over 17 million today, precisely because economic gravity overrode bureaucratic intent. What worked far better, arguably, was India's Smart Cities Mission, which invested roughly 2 trillion rupees in upgrading 100 secondary cities to redistribute population pressure organically — a strategy that addresses the root cause.

Link: So rather than limiting migration, governments would be wiser to invest in regional development and improve urban infrastructure, allowing demographic flows to self-regulate through better opportunities elsewhere.
Q2: Are smart cities solving real problems?

Point: Frankly, while smart city initiatives have delivered tangible benefits in specific domains, much of the hype around them is, in my opinion, technological solutionism dressed up as urban policy.

Explain: The crux of the matter is that the most pressing urban challenges — affordable housing, social cohesion, climate resilience — are fundamentally political and economic problems, not data problems. Deploying ten thousand IoT sensors does virtually nothing to address a housing crisis driven by speculative investment.

Example: Songdo in South Korea is a case in point: marketed as the world's first smart city with a $40 billion investment, it remains roughly half-empty more than a decade after completion because planners optimised for technology rather than human-scale community. Conversely, Barcelona's "superblocks" programme — a relatively low-tech intervention that simply reclaimed streets from cars — reduced NOx emissions by 25% and added 6.6 hectares of green space, demonstrably improving quality of life.

Link: This suggests that the real urban innovations of our time are likely to be sociological rather than technological — which calls into question whether the smart city paradigm is even asking the right questions.
Q3: How will cities adapt to climate change?

Point: Urban climate adaptation, I would suggest, hinges on a fundamental shift from grey infrastructure towards what planners now call "urban resilience" — designing cities that are antifragile rather than merely robust.

Explain: The reality is that, with sea levels projected to rise by up to one metre by 2100 according to IPCC AR6, and heatwaves intensifying globally, retrofitting existing cities is no longer optional. Adaptation strategies typically fall into three categories: green infrastructure, water management, and density redistribution.

Example: Rotterdam provides perhaps the most instructive example, having invested over €600 million in "water plazas" — public squares that double as flood reservoirs during storms — alongside floating neighbourhoods like Schoonschip. Singapore, meanwhile, mandates that all new buildings achieve a Green Plot Ratio above 1.0, effectively requiring more vegetation than the building's footprint displaces. Vietnam's Mekong Delta cities, by contrast, face a far thornier challenge given that roughly 12 million people may need relocating by 2050.

Link: Ultimately, adaptation will demand unprecedented coordination between municipal authorities, residents, and the private sector — and cities that fail to embrace circular economy principles may simply become uninhabitable.

4. Transcript (≈600 words)

> Good afternoon. Today's lecture interrogates three buzzwords that dominate contemporary urbanism: the smart city, gentrification, and urban resilience. Each, I will argue, conceals as much as it reveals.

> Let me begin with the smart-city paradigm. Marketed by technology vendors as a turnkey solution to gridlock, pollution and inefficient service delivery, it promises a metropolis governed by sensors, algorithms and real-time dashboards. Songdo in South Korea and Masdar in the United Arab Emirates remain the canonical, if rather sterile, examples. The omission, however, is glaring. These platforms generate vast streams of granular citizen data, raising acute questions of algorithmic governance and surveillance. Who, precisely, owns the data harvested from your commute, your utility bill, your kerbside rubbish bin?

> Now, gentrification. The orthodox account frames it as benign revitalization — dilapidated districts rebranded, cafés sprouting, crime falling. The shadow account is less flattering. Once affluent newcomers move in, property taxes and rents escalate, exorbitant asking prices push long-term, low-income residents to the periphery, and the cultural identity of the neighbourhood is, in the bluntest sense, hollowed out. The British sociologist Ruth Glass coined the term in 1964, observing precisely this dynamic in Islington. Six decades later, the mechanism is global.

> Finally, urban resilience. After Hurricane Sandy and the COVID-19 disruption, planners embraced resilience as a master concept — the capacity of a city to absorb shocks. But resilience for whom? Sea walls that shield Manhattan's financial district may divert flooding toward poorer outer boroughs. Resilience, like gentrification, is distributionally uneven.

Right, figure three — but before the displacement flows, I want to inject a case study that ties my three buzzwords into a single, rather damning knot. Cast your mind to Toronto's Quayside project, the waterfront development that Sidewalk Labs — a Google sibling — proposed to build from, as they put it, "the internet up". On paper it was the smart-city dream made concrete: sensors in the pavement, adaptive heated walkways, ubiquitous data harvesting to optimise everything from bin collection to crowd flow. And yet, in 2020, the whole venture collapsed. Why? Well, a citizens' coalition, led by figures like Bianca Wylie, mounted a sustained revolt over precisely the question I posed earlier — who owns the data, and who governs the algorithm? The technology, it transpired, was never the obstacle. Democratic legitimacy was. [pause]

What complicates the gentrification story, meanwhile, is a more recent and rather sinister mutation that scholars now call "green gentrification". The mechanism is, um, almost perverse: a city installs a flagship park, a restored waterfront, a network of cycle lanes — all impeccably sustainable, all resilience-enhancing — and the very amenity inflates surrounding land values, expelling the low-income residents it was ostensibly built to serve. New York's High Line is the canonical example. So sustainability and displacement, far from being opposites, can be two faces of the same coin. [pause]

A further consideration is that resilience itself is increasingly being privatised. After Sandy, some Manhattan towers commissioned their own flood barriers and backup grids — "resilience for those who can pay" — while public infrastructure for the outer boroughs languished. The city fragments, if you like, into an archipelago of secured enclaves and exposed peripheries. [pause]

So smart, green and resilient — three virtues that, unexamined, conspire to entrench advantage rather than redistribute it. And that convergence is precisely the dilemma I want planners to sit with — let me flag the key policy implication…
> The take-home is uncomfortable: smart, revitalised and resilient cities can still be socially regressive. Now, turning to figure three, which maps displacement flows…

The line graph compares the urban population, in millions, of four megacities - Tokyo, Delhi, Lagos and Sao Paulo - over a fifty-year period from 1975 to 2025.

Overall, while Tokyo retained its status as the largest urban agglomeration throughout, its growth plateaued, whereas Delhi and Lagos underwent the most dramatic megacity expansion. Sao Paulo, by contrast, followed a comparatively moderate urbanisation trajectory across the period.

In 1975, Tokyo already housed approximately 26.6 million inhabitants, dwarfing the other three cities, which ranged between 1.9 and 10.7 million. Delhi, however, surged almost eight-fold, climbing from 4.4 million to roughly 33.8 million and nearly converging with Tokyo by 2025. (f) Bài mẫu — BAND 8.0 (~194 từ)
The line graph charts the urban population, in millions, of four megacities - Tokyo, Delhi, Lagos and Sao Paulo - between 1975 and 2025.

Overall, a clear contrast emerges between the mature agglomeration and the emerging ones: Tokyo, though consistently the most populous, all but plateaued, whereas Delhi and Lagos expanded explosively and Sao Paulo advanced at a more sedate pace. The half-century thus narrowed a once-vast gulf between the established and the rising megacities.

Tokyo opened far ahead, at 26.6 million, and crept up to a peak of 38.1 million in 2015 before slipping to 37.2 million - a trajectory typical of a saturated, ageing economy. Sao Paulo traced a gentler arc, rising steadily from 10.7 to 22.4 million.

The Asian and African cities, by contrast, transformed the picture entirely. Delhi rocketed almost eight-fold, from 4.4 to 33.8 million, all but converging on Tokyo by 2025; Lagos, climbing off a negligible 1.9 million to some 21.0 million, registered the steepest relative ascent of all, drawing almost level with Sao Paulo by 2025 yet never overtaking it. blocks.text: (7) Bài luận mẫu — BAND 7.0 (~272 words)

Urban overcrowding has emerged as a defining issue of the twenty-first century, particularly across rapidly developing economies. In my view, this phenomenon stems chiefly from unchecked rural-to-urban migration and inadequate municipal planning, although a combination of targeted policies could reasonably alleviate the pressure.

It is rural migration, more than any other factor, that has paved the way for today's overcrowded metropolises. Young workers tend to flock to capital cities in search of better employment opportunities and superior educational amenities, leaving the countryside hollowed out. A second cause, arguably just as significant, is the failure of municipal authorities to expand transport infrastructure at the same pace as population growth. In many fast-growing cities, the subway network has barely changed in fifteen years even though the population has nearly doubled, a clear case of planning lagging behind demographic reality.

Turning to solutions, governments should, in my opinion, decentralise economic activity by developing satellite towns with their own industries and universities. This would, to some extent, redirect migrants away from saturated centres. Equally important is heavy subsidisation of mass transit; only when buses and trains become more reliable than private cars will commuters genuinely abandon their vehicles. The 15-minute city model, which Paris has experimented with, also seems a promising blueprint, as it ensures residents can reach work, schools and healthcare within walking distance.

In conclusion, the overcrowding crisis is largely driven by migration patterns and weak infrastructure planning, and it is through decentralisation and investment in public transit that meaningful improvement can occur. While no single measure can solve the problem overnight, a coordinated approach could plausibly relieve the strain that megacities currently face.
(8) Bài luận mẫu — BAND 8.0 (~309 words)

Few urban phenomena are as pressing as the relentless overcrowding of contemporary cities, a trend driven by intersecting economic and demographic forces. While the underlying causes are well documented, the solutions demand far greater political will than is typically acknowledged.

The principal driver, it would appear, is the powerful economic pull of metropolises, where wages, healthcare amenities and cosmopolitan lifestyles vastly outstrip those of rural regions. Compounding this is the chronic inability of municipal authorities to scale infrastructure in step with arrivals; the result is gridlock, the proliferation of dilapidated slums, and rising psychological alienation among long-term residents. Not only does inadequate planning intensify daily commutes, but it also widens the chasm between affluent enclaves and marginalised peripheries, a divide that fuels long-term social instability.

A multifaceted response is required. The strategic decentralisation of economic activity, through the construction of satellite hubs with their own employment ecosystems, could plausibly redirect migration flows. Complementing this, the introduction of congestion charging, with Stockholm and London as instructive precedents, has been shown to curb private car usage while generating revenue for transit expansion. Equally compelling is the 15-minute city framework, under which essential services are reachable on foot, thereby reducing reliance on motorised commuting and, in the process, lowering the carbon footprint of the urban core. So overwhelming is the case for investment in mass transit that any government failing to subsidise it heavily risks condemning its cities to permanent gridlock, while squandering the agglomeration benefits that drew migrants in the first place.

In conclusion, the overcrowding crisis is, in essence, a planning failure rather than an inevitable consequence of growth. Through the deliberate distribution of opportunity, the disincentivisation of private vehicles and the redesign of neighbourhoods around walkability, policymakers can, in all likelihood, restore liveability to the urban environment, provided, of course, that short-term electoral pressures do not derail long-term strategy.
(9) Phân tích nâng band 7 → 8

•  Band 8 dùng đảo ngữ tầng cao ('Not only does inadequate planning... but it also...', 'So overwhelming is the case... that...') liên tục, trong khi Band 7 chỉ có một cleft 'It is rural migration... that...'.

•  Band 8 đưa lexis bậc Band 8 ('psychological alienation', 'affluent enclaves', 'dilapidated slums', 'disincentivisation') và nominalisation dày ('the strategic decentralisation of...', 'the redesign of neighbourhoods around walkability'), nâng Lexical Resource.

•  Band 8 khung hóa lại vấn đề ('in essence, a planning failure rather than an inevitable consequence of growth') và hedge tinh tế ('it would appear', 'in all likelihood', 'provided, of course, that...'), nâng Task Response và Coherence một bậc.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Sự cải tạo khu đô thị cũ khiến giá nhà đất tăng vọt, đẩy cư dân thu nhập thấp ra khỏi khu vực.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> **Gentrification** frequently displaces long-standing low-income communities, exacerbating urban inequality.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'gentry' (tầng lớp thượng lưu) + -fication → biến khu phố thành nơi ở của người khá giả.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Gentrification' không đồng nghĩa hoàn toàn với 'revitalization' — gentrification nhấn mạnh mặt trái (đẩy người nghèo ra ngoài), còn revitalization trung tính hơn.
vocabulary.definition_en: the process of renovating a deteriorated urban area, typically raising property values and displacing lower-income residents
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự cải tạo đô thị làm tăng giá, đẩy người thu nhập thấp ra ngoài
vocabulary.example: Gentrification frequently displaces long-standing low-income communities, exacerbating urban inequality.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'gentry' (tầng lớp thượng lưu) + -fication → biến khu phố thành nơi ở của người khá giả.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Tình trạng tắc nghẽn giao thông nghiêm trọng khiến không phương tiện nào di chuyển được.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Chronic traffic congestion has become an intractable feature of sprawling metropolitan areas, often escalating into full **gridlock** at peak hours.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'grid' (mạng lưới đường) bị 'locked' (khoá cứng) → xe cộ đứng im, không nhúc nhích.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Gridlock' là danh từ không đếm được, không có dạng số nhiều 'gridlocks' khi chỉ hiện tượng chung.
vocabulary.definition_en: a severe traffic jam in which no vehicle can move in any direction
vocabulary.definition_vi: tình trạng tắc nghẽn giao thông hoàn toàn
vocabulary.example: Chronic traffic congestion has become an intractable feature of sprawling metropolitan areas, often escalating into full gridlock at peak hours.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'grid' (mạng lưới đường) bị 'locked' (khoá cứng) → xe cộ đứng im, không nhúc nhích.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Xuống cấp, đổ nát vì bị bỏ bê lâu ngày, thường dùng cho nhà cửa hoặc khu phố cũ.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Unchecked arrivals fuel the proliferation of **dilapidated** slums on the periphery of the city.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'lapis' (đá) trong gốc Latin gợi 'từng viên đá rơi vỡ' → công trình mục nát dần.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Dilapidated' chỉ dùng cho vật thể (nhà cửa, công trình), không dùng để tả người bị suy sụp.
vocabulary.definition_en: (of a building or object) in a state of disrepair or ruin as a result of age or neglect
vocabulary.definition_vi: xuống cấp, đổ nát (do bỏ bê lâu ngày)
vocabulary.example: Unchecked arrivals fuel the proliferation of dilapidated slums on the periphery of the city.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'lapis' (đá) trong gốc Latin liên quan đến 'rơi vỡ từng viên đá' → công trình mục nát dần.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Có mặt ở khắp mọi nơi, cực kỳ phổ biến đến mức không thể tránh khỏi.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Coffee shops have become **ubiquitous** in this city, with a branch on virtually every corner.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
gốc Latin 'ubique' (ở khắp mọi nơi) → ubiquitous → có mặt ở mọi ngóc ngách.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Ubiquitous' là tính từ tuyệt đối, tránh dùng với 'very' hay 'more' vì bản thân từ đã mang nghĩa cực đại.
vocabulary.definition_en: existing or appearing everywhere at the same time; extremely common
vocabulary.definition_vi: có mặt khắp nơi, phổ biến ở mọi chỗ
vocabulary.example: Coffee shops have become ubiquitous in this city, with a branch on virtually every corner.
vocabulary.memory_hook: gốc Latin 'ubique' (ở khắp mọi nơi) → ubiquitous → có mặt ở mọi ngóc ngách.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Sự hồi sinh, cải tạo một khu vực đô thị để nó trở nên sống động, thịnh vượng trở lại.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The neighbourhood has somehow managed to **revitalize** itself without succumbing to aggressive gentrification, retaining its cultural identity.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
re- (lại) + vital (sức sống) → thổi lại sức sống cho khu phố cũ.
vocabulary.common_error: British spelling ưu tiên là 'revitalisation' (với -s-), 'revitalization' (-z-) là biến thể Mỹ; cả hai đều gặp trong tài liệu học thuật quốc tế.
vocabulary.definition_en: the action of restoring vitality to something, especially an urban area, making it active and prosperous again
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự hồi sinh, cải tạo (khu vực đô thị) trở nên sống động trở lại
vocabulary.example: The neighbourhood has somehow managed to revitalize itself without succumbing to aggressive gentrification, retaining its cultural identity.
vocabulary.memory_hook: re- (lại) + vital (sức sống) → thổi lại sức sống cho khu phố cũ.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Cảm giác cô lập, lạc lõng, đánh mất bản sắc, đặc biệt trong môi trường đô thị đông đúc.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The relentless pace and overcrowding of urban life can take a considerable toll on residents' wellbeing, breeding a quiet sense of **alienation**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'alien' (người xa lạ) → alienation → cảm giác trở thành người xa lạ giữa đám đông.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Alienation' đi với giới từ 'from' khi chỉ rõ đối tượng: 'alienation from society', không phải 'alienation of society'.
vocabulary.definition_en: a feeling of isolation, disconnection, or loss of identity, particularly within a large impersonal environment
vocabulary.definition_vi: cảm giác cô lập, lạc lõng, mất kết nối (thường trong môi trường đô thị)
vocabulary.example: The relentless pace and overcrowding of urban life can take a considerable toll on residents' wellbeing, breeding a quiet sense of alienation.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'alien' (người ngoài hành tinh/xa lạ) → alienation → cảm giác trở thành người xa lạ giữa đám đông.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Thuộc về thành phố hoặc chính quyền địa phương, đặc biệt trong việc cung cấp dịch vụ công.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> **Municipal** authorities have failed to scale infrastructure in step with population growth.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'muni-' gợi 'municipality' (thành phố tự quản) → municipal = việc của chính quyền thành phố.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Municipal' là tính từ, không dùng như danh từ; danh từ tương ứng là 'municipality' (đô thị tự quản).
vocabulary.definition_en: relating to a city or town or its local governing body, especially regarding public services
vocabulary.definition_vi: thuộc về thành phố/thị trấn, thuộc chính quyền địa phương
vocabulary.example: Municipal authorities have failed to scale infrastructure in step with population growth.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'muni-' liên quan 'municipality' (thành phố tự quản) → municipal = việc của chính quyền thành phố.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Nhà ở có mức giá phù hợp với khả năng chi trả của người lao động bình thường.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The government has pledged to build more **affordable housing** to tackle the housing crisis.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'afford' (đủ khả năng chi trả) + housing → nhà ở mà người bình thường đủ tiền mua.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Affordable housing' luôn không đếm được (uncountable); không thêm 's' hay dùng mạo từ 'an' trước nó.
vocabulary.definition_en: housing that is priced within the financial reach of ordinary working people
vocabulary.definition_vi: nhà ở giá phải chăng, phù hợp túi tiền người lao động phổ thông
vocabulary.example: The government has pledged to build more affordable housing to tackle the housing crisis.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'afford' (đủ khả năng chi trả) + housing → nhà ở mà người bình thường đủ tiền mua.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Quá trình một tỷ lệ dân số ngày càng lớn chuyển đến sinh sống tại thành thị.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Rapid **urbanisation** is placing immense pressure on housing, transport and public infrastructure.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
urban (thành thị) + -isation (quá trình) → quá trình biến vùng đất thành đô thị.
vocabulary.common_error: British spelling là 'urbanisation' (-s-); tránh viết lẫn 'urbanization' (Mỹ) trong bài thi theo chuẩn Anh.
vocabulary.definition_en: the process by which an increasing proportion of a population comes to live in towns and cities
vocabulary.definition_vi: quá trình đô thị hoá
vocabulary.example: Rapid urbanisation is placing immense pressure on housing, transport and public infrastructure.
vocabulary.memory_hook: urban (thành thị) + -isation (quá trình) → quá trình biến vùng đất thành đô thị.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Tình trạng quá tải, ùn tắc, thường dùng để chỉ giao thông đông đúc gây chậm trễ nghiêm trọng.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Chronic traffic **congestion** has become an intractable feature of sprawling metropolitan areas.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'con-' (cùng nhau) + 'gest' (chất đống) → mọi thứ dồn ứ lại cùng một chỗ → tắc nghẽn.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Congestion' không đếm được; nói 'severe congestion', không nói 'a congestion' hay 'congestions'.
vocabulary.definition_en: a state of overcrowding, especially of traffic, causing severe delays
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự ùn tắc, quá tải (thường chỉ giao thông)
vocabulary.example: Chronic traffic congestion has become an intractable feature of sprawling metropolitan areas.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'con-' (cùng nhau) + 'gest' (mang, chất) → mọi thứ dồn ứ lại cùng một chỗ → tắc nghẽn.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Hệ thống cơ sở vật chất nền tảng (giao thông, điện, nước) cần thiết để xã hội vận hành.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Municipal authorities have failed to scale **infrastructure** in step with population growth.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'infra-' (bên dưới) + 'structure' (cấu trúc) → những cấu trúc nền tảng nâng đỡ cả thành phố.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Infrastructure' không đếm được; không nói 'infrastructures' hay 'an infrastructure' khi chỉ khái niệm chung.
vocabulary.definition_en: the basic physical systems and structures (transport, power, water) needed for a society to function
vocabulary.definition_vi: cơ sở hạ tầng
vocabulary.example: Municipal authorities have failed to scale infrastructure in step with population growth.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'infra-' (bên dưới) + 'structure' (cấu trúc) → những cấu trúc nền tảng nằm bên dưới, nâng đỡ cả thành phố.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Sự lan rộng thiếu quy hoạch của đô thị ra các vùng đất nông thôn xung quanh.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Relentless peri-urban growth propelled Lagos to over twenty million inhabitants, a textbook case of unchecked urban **sprawl**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
hình dung một người 'sprawl' (duỗi tay chân lộn xộn) ra sàn → thành phố cũng 'duỗi' ra vô tổ chức.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Sprawl' mang hàm ý tiêu cực (thiếu quy hoạch, lãng phí đất); tránh dùng thay cho 'growth' hay 'expansion' trung tính.
vocabulary.definition_en: the uncontrolled, low-density expansion of an urban area into surrounding countryside
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự lan rộng đô thị thiếu quy hoạch ra vùng ven
vocabulary.example: Relentless peri-urban growth propelled Lagos to over twenty million inhabitants, a textbook case of unchecked urban sprawl.
vocabulary.memory_hook: hình dung một người 'sprawl' (nằm dài, duỗi tay chân lộn xộn) ra sàn → thành phố cũng 'duỗi' ra vô tổ chức.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Mức độ một nơi chốn dễ chịu và thuận tiện để sinh sống.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Investment in green spaces and public amenities is pivotal to enhancing a city's **liveability**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'live' (sống) + '-able' (có thể) + '-ity' (tính chất) → tính "sống được" thoải mái của một thành phố.
vocabulary.common_error: British spelling giữ nguyên 'e' trước hậu tố: 'liveable/liveability', không lược thành 'livable' như tiếng Mỹ.
vocabulary.definition_en: the degree to which a place is pleasant and practical to live in
vocabulary.definition_vi: khả năng đáng sống, mức độ dễ chịu để sinh sống của một nơi
vocabulary.example: Investment in green spaces and public amenities is pivotal to enhancing a city's liveability.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'live' (sống) + '-able' (có thể) + '-ity' (tính chất) → tính chất 'sống được' thoải mái của một thành phố.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Tình trạng một nơi có quá nhiều người, gây khó chịu và áp lực lên nguồn lực.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Urban **overcrowding** has emerged as a defining issue of the twenty-first century, particularly across rapidly developing economies.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'over-' (quá mức) + 'crowding' (đông đúc) → đông đến mức quá tải.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Overcrowding' là danh từ trừu tượng không đếm được; tính từ tương ứng là 'overcrowded' ('an overcrowded city').
vocabulary.definition_en: the state of having too many people in a place, causing discomfort or strain on resources
vocabulary.definition_vi: tình trạng quá tải dân số
vocabulary.example: Urban overcrowding has emerged as a defining issue of the twenty-first century, particularly across rapidly developing economies.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'over-' (quá mức) + 'crowding' (đông đúc) → đông đến mức quá tải.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Tiện ích công cộng hữu ích của một khu vực, ví dụ chợ, công viên, phòng khám.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Essential **amenities** like markets, cafes, and clinics are all within a fifteen-minute stroll.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
gốc Latin 'amoenus' (dễ chịu) → amenity → những thứ làm cuộc sống dễ chịu hơn.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Amenity' thường dùng ở số nhiều 'amenities' khi liệt kê các tiện ích của một khu vực.
vocabulary.definition_en: a desirable or useful feature or facility of a building or place, such as a shop, park or clinic
vocabulary.definition_vi: tiện ích công cộng
vocabulary.example: Essential amenities like markets, cafes, and clinics are all within a fifteen-minute stroll.
vocabulary.memory_hook: gốc Latin 'amoenus' (dễ chịu) → amenity → những thứ làm cuộc sống dễ chịu hơn.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Nỗ lực, vật lộn để giải quyết hoặc thấu hiểu một vấn đề khó khăn.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> City planners must **grapple with** the challenge of housing millions of new arrivals without sacrificing liveability.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'grapple' vốn nghĩa 'vật lộn tay đôi' → grapple with a problem → ôm lấy vấn đề mà vật lộn tìm cách giải quyết.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Grapple with' luôn cần giới từ 'with' theo sau; không bỏ giới từ khi đứng trước tân ngữ.
vocabulary.definition_en: to try hard to deal with or understand a difficult problem
vocabulary.definition_vi: vật lộn, nỗ lực giải quyết (một vấn đề khó khăn)
vocabulary.example: City planners must grapple with the challenge of housing millions of new arrivals without sacrificing liveability.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'grapple' vốn nghĩa 'vật lộn tay đôi' → grapple with a problem → ôm lấy vấn đề mà vật lộn tìm cách giải quyết.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Cách gọi ẩn dụ chỉ thành phố đông đúc, nhiều bê tông, thiếu cây xanh, gây cảm giác ngột ngạt.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> With very few parks and trees, the city centre feels like a depressing **concrete jungle**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'concrete' (bê tông) + 'jungle' (rừng rậm) → những toà nhà bê tông san sát như cây rừng chằng chịt.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Concrete jungle' là cụm cố định (idiom); không tách rời hay chia số nhiều 'concrete jungles' trừ khi so sánh nhiều thành phố.
vocabulary.definition_en: a large, densely built city, seen as an unpleasant or oppressive place to live because of the lack of greenery
vocabulary.definition_vi: rừng bê tông (chỉ đô thị chật chội, thiếu cây xanh)
vocabulary.example: With very few parks and trees, the city centre feels like a depressing concrete jungle.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'concrete' (bê tông) + 'jungle' (rừng rậm) → những toà nhà bê tông san sát như cây rừng chằng chịt.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Tạo điều kiện thuận lợi, mở đường cho một sự phát triển hoặc thành tựu trong tương lai.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The new metro line will **pave the way for** further economic development in the suburbs.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'pave' (lát đường) + 'the way' (con đường) → lát sẵn con đường cho điều gì đó thuận lợi xảy ra.
vocabulary.common_error: Luôn theo sau bằng giới từ 'for', không phải 'to': 'pave the way for change', không nói 'pave the way to change' (trừ trường hợp danh động từ).
vocabulary.definition_en: to create conditions that make a future development or achievement possible
vocabulary.definition_vi: mở đường, tạo tiền đề cho (điều gì đó xảy ra)
vocabulary.example: The new metro line will pave the way for further economic development in the suburbs.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'pave' (lát đường) + 'the way' (con đường) → lát sẵn con đường cho điều gì đó thuận lợi xảy ra.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Diễn tả điều gì đó rất hợp sở thích hoặc sở trường của một người.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> This new job in urban architecture is **right up my street**, given my background in design.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
hình dung con phố (street) ngay trước nhà mình → cái gì 'ngay trên phố của mình' thì rất quen thuộc, hợp với mình.
vocabulary.common_error: Idiom kiểu Anh dùng 'street', trong khi tiếng Anh Mỹ thường dùng 'alley'; tránh trộn lẫn hai biến thể trong cùng một bài viết học thuật.
vocabulary.definition_en: exactly the kind of thing that someone likes, enjoys, or is skilled at
vocabulary.definition_vi: đúng sở trường, đúng ý thích của ai đó
vocabulary.example: This new job in urban architecture is right up my street, given my background in design.
vocabulary.memory_hook: hình dung con phố (street) ngay trước nhà mình → cái gì 'ngay trên phố của mình' thì rất quen thuộc, hợp với mình.

Tổng chi phí cần thiết để trang trải cuộc sống hằng ngày như nhà ở, ăn uống, đi lại.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The skyrocketing **cost of living** makes it nearly impossible for students to save money.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'cost' (chi phí) + 'of living' (để sống) → tổng chi phí cần để duy trì cuộc sống hằng ngày.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Cost of living' không đếm được và không có mạo từ 'a' đứng trước khi nói chung chung; chỉ thêm 'the' khi cụ thể hoá.
vocabulary.definition_en: the amount of money needed to cover basic expenses such as housing, food and transport in a particular place
vocabulary.definition_vi: chi phí sinh hoạt
vocabulary.example: The skyrocketing cost of living makes it nearly impossible for students to save money.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'cost' (chi phí) + 'of living' (để sống) → tổng chi phí cần để duy trì cuộc sống hằng ngày.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Tình trạng khủng hoảng do thiếu hụt nghiêm trọng nhà ở giá phải chăng.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The government has pledged to build more affordable homes to tackle the **housing crisis**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'housing' (nhà ở) + 'crisis' (khủng hoảng) → tình trạng khan hiếm nhà ở trầm trọng.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Housing crisis' viết liền hai danh từ ghép, không thêm giới từ 'of' ở giữa như 'crisis of housing'.
vocabulary.definition_en: a severe shortage of affordable housing that leaves many people unable to find suitable accommodation
vocabulary.definition_vi: cuộc khủng hoảng nhà ở (thiếu nhà giá phải chăng)
vocabulary.example: The government has pledged to build more affordable homes to tackle the housing crisis.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'housing' (nhà ở) + 'crisis' (khủng hoảng) → tình trạng khan hiếm nhà ở trầm trọng.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Đắt đỏ, cắt cổ, cao đến mức phi lý, thường dùng để mô tả giá cả hoặc chi phí.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Rent prices in the downtown area have become **exorbitantly** high, pushing long-term residents to the periphery.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'ex-' (vượt ra ngoài) + 'orbit' (quỹ đạo) → giá cả vượt ra khỏi quỹ đạo hợp lý, cao đến mức phi lý.
vocabulary.common_error: Đừng nhầm 'exorbitant' (đắt đỏ vô lý) với 'exuberant' (tràn đầy năng lượng, hào hứng) — hai từ gần âm nhưng nghĩa khác hẳn.
vocabulary.definition_en: (of a price or amount charged) unreasonably high
vocabulary.definition_vi: cắt cổ, đắt đỏ quá mức hợp lý
vocabulary.example: Rent prices in the downtown area have become exorbitantly high, pushing long-term residents to the periphery.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'ex-' (vượt ra ngoài) + 'orbit' (quỹ đạo) → giá cả vượt ra khỏi quỹ đạo hợp lý, cao đến mức phi lý.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Giàu có, sung túc, có nhiều tiền của.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Once **affluent** newcomers move in, property taxes and rents escalate, pushing long-term, low-income residents to the periphery.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'af-' + 'fluere' (chảy, gốc Latin) → tiền của 'chảy vào' dồi dào → giàu có, sung túc.
vocabulary.common_error: Đừng nhầm 'affluent' (giàu có) với 'effluent' (nước thải) — hai từ chỉ khác một chữ cái nhưng nghĩa hoàn toàn trái ngược sắc thái.
vocabulary.definition_en: having a great deal of money or wealth; prosperous
vocabulary.definition_vi: giàu có, sung túc
vocabulary.example: Once affluent newcomers move in, property taxes and rents escalate, pushing long-term, low-income residents to the periphery.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'af-' + 'fluere' (chảy, gốc Latin) → tiền của 'chảy vào' dồi dào → giàu có, sung túc.

Sự phân tán hoạt động kinh tế hoặc dân cư ra khỏi trung tâm để giảm áp lực lên đô thị lớn.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The strategic **decentralisation** of economic activity, through the construction of satellite hubs with their own employment ecosystems, could plausibly redirect migration flows.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
de- (tách khỏi) + 'central' (trung tâm) → tách hoạt động ra khỏi trung tâm, san đều ra nhiều nơi.
vocabulary.common_error: British spelling là 'decentralisation' (-s-); tránh viết 'decentralization' (Mỹ) trong bài thi IELTS chuẩn Anh.
vocabulary.definition_en: the transfer of activity, control or population away from a central, dominant location to multiple smaller centres
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự phân tán, giãn dân/giãn quyền lực ra khỏi trung tâm
vocabulary.example: The strategic decentralisation of economic activity, through the construction of satellite hubs with their own employment ecosystems, could plausibly redirect migration flows.
vocabulary.memory_hook: de- (tách khỏi) + 'central' (trung tâm) → tách hoạt động ra khỏi trung tâm, san đều ra nhiều nơi.
